clue.text: Not the dictator's complaint

parts.note: a dictator here is someone who dictates letters to a secretary rather than writing them, so the ache of a hand that writes all day never troubles him

explanation.surface: A tyrant is apparently free of some particular ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant, but it means a person dictating letters; the one holding the pen gets the aching hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The ache from long handwriting is the penman's affliction, which someone who only dictates escapes.

clue.text: Where not to seek Fire's highlights?

definitions.text: Where not to seek Fire's highlights?

parts.words: Where not to seek Fire's highlights?
parts.note: split as two words, a candle or lamp with its wick turned down is no place for bright flames; the whole is also an Irish county name

explanation.surface: A question about some place where a fire's brightest moments cannot be found.
explanation.walkthrough: WICKLOW is a county in the Republic of Ireland; read as WICK LOW it describes a flame turned down, so no fire's highlights there.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp whose wick is low gives a dim flame, so bright points of fire are absent; the county's name spells that phrase.

clue.text: Purposes' to get in Spanish wines

definitions.note: plural noun, aims or objectives; the apostrophe is printed on the page

parts.note: taken as written
tent is an old name for a deep red Spanish wine, so tents are Spanish wines

explanation.surface: Somebody's aims are to get into a stock of Spanish wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' is a link joining the definition to the wordplay; TENT, a dark red wine from Spain, is an old word now met mainly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Intents are aims or plans, the same as purposes.

clue.text: Strange Oriental sex vices are too much

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for East, so eastern or Oriental gives E

indicators.note: something strange is odd or out of order, so the letters that follow get rearranged

explanation.surface: Exotic eastern vices of a sexual kind are said to be beyond the pale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges E (Oriental) with SEX and VICES, nine letters giving the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive means beyond a proper limit; things that are too much exceed what is reasonable.

clue.text: Jack's the boy to catch mackerel

definitions.meaning: Jack ... is the nursery-rhyme man who could eat no fat, so his surname names the boy
the proverb 'a ... to catch a mackerel' means a small bait risked to win a bigger prize

explanation.surface: Young Jack is the lad to send out to land a mackerel.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from British sayings: the nursery rhyme 'Jack Sprat could eat no fat', and the proverb about using a small fish as bait for a bigger one.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack's surname in the rhyme; and the small herring-like fish used as bait in the proverb about catching larger prey.

clue.text: Bird followed by a Scot, an ugly customer

parts.note: a ruff is a wading bird of the sandpiper family
Ian is the Scottish form of John, standing in for any Scotsman

explanation.surface: A bird is accompanied by a Scotsman who is not a pleasant character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'followed by' joins the pieces in the clue's order; IAN is a stock crossword Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruffian is a violent, brutish man, which an ugly customer is in British slang for a dangerous person.

clue.text: Cocktail in the armoury

definitions.meaning: a mixed drink of gin and vermouth
the ...-Henry was a breech-loading rifle of the Victorian British army, kept in an armoury

explanation.surface: Someone is mixing drinks in a weapons store.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the Martini-Henry rifle used by the British army in the late 1800s.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin and vermouth drink shares its name with a Victorian service rifle stored among weapons.

clue.text: What's made in an hour with a single knot

definitions.text: What's made in an hour with a single knot

parts.words: What's made in an hour with a single knot
parts.note: a knot is a speed of one sea-mile per hour, so a vessel at one knot covers a certain distance each hour

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what a person can make in an hour by tying just one knot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knot' suggests tying string, but it is the unit of speed at sea: one knot covers one of these distances every hour.
explanation.definitionFit: The knot is defined as a speed of exactly one sea-mile per hour, so that distance is what one knot achieves in sixty minutes.

clue.text: Unusual case, citizen turns into hermit

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, here telling the solver to rearrange the letters

parts.note: CIT is a dated abbreviation for citizen, a townsperson

explanation.surface: An odd legal case in which a city resident becomes a recluse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges CASE with CIT (citizen); 'turns into' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascetic renounces comfort and pleasure, as a hermit living in solitude does.

clue.text: Improves classes for engineers

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
a form is a school class in British usage

explanation.surface: Somebody upgrades the training courses on offer to engineers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. FORM is the British word for a school class or year group.
explanation.definitionFit: To reform something is to make it better, so reforms is a verb meaning makes better.

clue.text: Are they used to reveal contents of cupboards?

definitions.text: Are they used to reveal contents of cupboards?

parts.words: Are they used to reveal contents of cupboards?
parts.note: the idiom 'a skeleton in the cupboard' is a hidden family secret; master keys that open any lock might expose such bones

explanation.surface: A question about the tools for opening cupboards to see what is inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom is 'a skeleton in the cupboard' (American 'closet'): a shameful secret. The answer is the master key that opens many locks, read as keys to the skeletons.
explanation.definitionFit: A master key fitting many locks would open any cupboard, including those hiding skeletons.

clue.text: Gifts of money in former days

definitions.meaning: in the ancient world a talent was a large unit of weight and of money

explanation.surface: Presents of cash in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: The sense of natural ability comes from the parable of the talents, where coins were entrusted to servants.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural aptitudes; and an ancient unit of currency, as in the biblical parable.

clue.text: Possible danger of an inadequate freeze

parts.note: thin means meagre or insufficient, as a thin excuse
ice is what water becomes when it freezes

explanation.surface: A weak frost might bring some hazard with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text adds 'inane,' which the printed page lacks. 'of an' is a link; 'on thin ice' is the idiom for being in a risky position.
explanation.definitionFit: Skating on a fragile frozen surface risks falling through, so it stands for a precarious situation.

clue.text: A hundred birds on the chimneys

definitions.note: the definition names the things found on top of the chimneys, a plural noun

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
owls are nocturnal birds of prey

explanation.surface: A great flock of birds perched on rooftop stacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer by where it sits: hooded metal covers fitted on chimney tops.
explanation.definitionFit: A hood-shaped cover fitted on top of a chimney pot to aid the draught; these sit on chimneys.

clue.text: In foreign currency I've found encouragement

parts.note: the cent is a coin in American and other currencies, foreign to a British setter
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone has discovered an inducement in money from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found' is a link; the pieces simply run in order.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive is a motivating inducement, something that spurs a person on.

clue.text: A cart a man can adapt for travel by water

definitions.note: the definition describes a vessel by its use, a craft made for crossing water

indicators.note: to adapt is to modify, so these letters are reshaped into a new word

explanation.surface: A man can convert a cart so it will float.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapt' rearranges the nine letters of A CART A MAN; 'can' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-hulled sailing boat, a vessel used for journeys on water.

clue.text: Presumably in doing this one goes flat out

definitions.text: Presumably in doing this one goes flat out

parts.words: Presumably in doing this one goes flat out
parts.note: flat out means at full effort; read literally, a flat, even surface is one that is horizontal throughout

explanation.surface: Explaining what it means to go flat out at something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat out' means with maximum effort, while 'level' also means flat; so doing one's utmost is read as being flat to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing one's utmost means going at full effort, which is going flat out; level also means flat.

clue.text: Portugal's prominent saint

parts.note: Cape St ... is the headland at the south-western tip of Portugal, a prominent point named for a saint

explanation.surface: Naming the leading holy figure of Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prominent' means famous on the surface but here it is a promontory: Cape St Vincent juts out from the Portuguese coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Vincent gives his name to Portugal's south-western cape, a jutting headland.

clue.text: Girl is perhaps to alter her name

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters may be put in another order, one possible arrangement among many

explanation.surface: A young woman might change what she is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the seven letters of TO ALTER; 'is' and 'her name' link the parts, with the girl's name the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, so it can stand for a girl.

clue.text: Two pages when turned back fail to disclose oil source

definitions.text: Two pages when turned back fail to disclose oil source

parts.words: Two pages when turned back fail to disclose oil source
parts.note: a single leaf has two pages; its name written backwards spells OIL OF, a phrase that stops short of saying what the oil comes from

explanation.surface: Turning back a couple of pages does not reveal where some oil came from.
explanation.walkthrough: A sheet folded once makes two pages. Its name reversed reads 'oil of', which leaves the oil's source unstated.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf of a book, printed on both sides, giving two numbered pages.

clue.text: Wearisome military duty

parts.note: soldiers' menial non-combat chores, such as cleaning and cookhouse work, carry a name that also means tiredness

explanation.surface: Tiring chores done in the army.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers' non-combat chores are called by this name, which also means weariness.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers' menial chores carry the same name as exhaustion, so the tiresome tasks share the word.

clue.text: One vessel under one pound, the African Queen ?

parts.note: L stands for a pound sterling, from Latin libra
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
SS stands for steamship, a vessel

explanation.surface: A boat beneath one pound note, as if it were the film The African Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' places ONE SS below L I. The African Queen is a 1951 boat film, but here it means the queen of beasts in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The female of the big cat, king of beasts, makes her the queen of the African wild.

clue.text: Takes no notice of re distribution of regions

indicators.note: redistribution means sharing out again in a new pattern, so the letters of the word that follows are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone disregards a proposal to reallocate territories.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 're-distribution', split across a line; it rearranges the seven letters of REGIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore is to disregard, paying no attention to something.

clue.text: Does this hit mean success or disaster ?

definitions.text: Does this hit mean success or disaster ?

parts.words: Does this hit mean success or disaster ?
parts.note: a show that is a huge hit is called by a word that also means a crash or catastrophic collapse, as well as a hard blow

explanation.surface: Asking whether a big hit is a triumph or a ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means a hard blow, a runaway success ('a smash hit') and a crash or financial collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: A forceful stroke; a runaway hit show; and a crash: the one word covers blow, triumph and ruin.

clue.text: Derbyshire town in need of a hairdresser ?

definitions.text: Derbyshire town in need of a hairdresser ?

parts.words: Derbyshire town in need of a hairdresser ?
parts.note: read as two words, a tangled strand of hair needs a hairdresser; joined, it is a spa town in the county of Derbyshire

explanation.surface: Asking which Derbyshire town is overdue a haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: Derbyshire is a county in the English Midlands; split as MAT LOCK, the town's name is a tangled tress that a hairdresser could sort out.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa town that is the county seat of Derbyshire, whose name splits into a matted tress.

clue.text: For Greek tragedy choose an artist

parts.note: to elect is to choose, by vote or otherwise
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: To select a painter for a production of a classical tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is a link. RA, a Royal Academician, is the standard crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Plays of this title by Sophocles and Euripides are classical Greek tragedies.

clue.text: Characteristic of Herries senior ?

parts.note: Hugh Walpole's novel Rogue Herries is named for its hero Francis Herries, the elder of the family saga, whose nickname names his chief trait

explanation.surface: Asking about a trait of the older Herries.
explanation.walkthrough: Rogue Herries (1930) is Hugh Walpole's novel about the Herries family of Cumberland; its patriarch is nicknamed Rogue, so his trait is roguish behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishonest, rascally conduct is the defining trait of the novel's patriarch nicknamed Rogue.

clue.text: They travel on foot in the rush hour

definitions.text: They travel on foot in the rush hour

parts.words: They travel on foot in the rush hour
parts.note: standing passengers on crowded trains and buses travel on their feet, gripping the loops overhead, rather than walking

explanation.surface: Describing commuters who walk to work at peak times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on foot' suggests walking, but these commuters ride standing up, holding a hanging strap because no seat is free.
explanation.definitionFit: Commuters without seats stand holding overhead loops, so they ride the train on their feet.
